newsitem.title: FRANCE: France says not asking for command of U.S. fleet.
newsitem.headline: France says not asking for command of U.S. fleet.

text.p: France said on Monday its demand for NATO's southern flank to be placed under a European commander did not mean that it was asking for control of the U.S. Sixth Fleet based in the Mediterranean sea region.

In an apparent concession in a row with Washington, that is holding up reform of the alliance, it said that the United States could relinquish NATO's southern command, AFSOUTH, while retaining command of the Sixth Fleet.
"We are not demanding that a European officer command the Sixth Fleet. It could be under direct U.S. command," Foreign Ministry spokesman Jacques Rummelhardt told a news briefing.

Rummelhardt said there was an agreement in principle on the European deputy to NATO's American Supreme Allied Commander, Europe (SACEUR), another aspect of the dispute. U.S. officials have said they accepted giving the European officer greater responsibility.

NATO's 16 foreign ministers are to meet in Brussels on Tuesday to give final approval to a new peace mission in Bosnia and review internal reforms necessary for the alliance's expansion plans in eastern Europe to go ahead.
Plans to reform the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) have been held up by a row between the United States and France over who is to command NATO's vital southern flank.
Ever since the alliance was set up in 1949, a U.S. officer has held the Naples-based southern command, which carries with it control of the U.S. Sixth Fleet.

Now, France is demanding that this post be handed over to a European, arguing that the issue goes to the heart of a U.S commitment to create a distinct European identity within the U.S.-dominated alliance.
The issue of U.S. forces being commanded by a foreigner is a sensitive one in the United States, and American leaders say they will never reliquish control of the Sixth Fleet.
Paris has hinted that the issue could delay its plan to rejoin NATO's military structure, which it left 30 years ago, and in turn delay the alliance's expansion plans.
